summary: Describes an LDAPv3 control that lets a client ask a directory server to return search results in pages instead of all at once. The client fetches one chunk at a time and asks for the next, which keeps large searches manageable. This is an informational memo, not a standard.

plainLanguage.summary: Imagine asking a librarian for every book about dogs. Instead of a giant pile, she hands you a few at a time and you ask for more when ready.

subtitle: A way for an LDAP client to pull search results one page at a time using an opaque cookie.

tldr.problem: An LDAP search can return a huge result set, which is hard on a client with limited resources or a low-bandwidth connection.
tldr.mechanism: The client attaches a paged results control with a page size and an empty cookie. The server answers with one page and a cookie, and the client sends that cookie back to get the next page.
tldr.outcome: The result set is retrieved in chunks until the server returns an empty cookie. It is an Informational memo, and it deliberately offers nothing more sophisticated than simple paging.

today: RFC 2696 is an Informational memo from September 1999. The metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: What the Control Is For
sections.content:
This memo describes an LDAPv3 control extension for simple paging of search results. It lets a client control the rate at which an LDAP server returns the results of a search.

The RFC says this may be useful when the client has limited resources and cannot process the entire result set, or when it is connected over a low-bandwidth connection. Other operations on the result set are not defined, and the extension is not designed to provide more sophisticated result set management.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of dumping a whole box of toys on the floor, the server hands you a few toys at a time so you are never overwhelmed.

sections.title: The Paged Results Control
sections.content:
The control is carried in the controls field of the LDAP message, in both the searchRequest and the searchResultDone messages. Its control type is the object identifier 1.2.840.113556.1.4.319, and criticality defaults to FALSE.

The control value is an OCTET STRING that wraps a BER-encoded SEQUENCE with two fields: size (an integer from 0 to maxInt) and cookie (an octet string). From the client, size is the requested page size. From the server, it is an estimate of the size of the whole result set.
sections.plainLanguage: The control is a small note stapled to the request. One part says how many items you want, and the other part is a claim ticket.

sections.title: Client and Server Interaction
sections.content:
To start, the client sends a search with the control, size set to the page size and a zero-length cookie. The page size may be greater than zero and less than the sizeLimit of the search. If the page size is greater than or equal to sizeLimit, the server should ignore the control, since one page is enough.

With every page, the server includes the control in searchResultDone. The size MAY be its estimate of the total entries, or zero if it cannot estimate. The cookie MUST be empty when there are no more entries, and otherwise is an octet string of the server's choosing used to resume the search.

The client MUST treat the cookie as opaque. To get the next page it MUST resend the request with everything identical except the messageID, the cookie and optionally the page size, using the cookie from the last searchResultDone. Once the sequence is complete the cookie MUST NOT be used again.

If the server does not support the control, it MUST return unsupportedCriticalExtension when the client marked it critical, and otherwise SHOULD ignore it.
sections.plainLanguage: You ask for three cards. The server gives you three and a numbered ticket. You hand back the ticket to get the next three, until it says there are no more.

sections.title: Abandoning, Limits and Changing Data
sections.content:
A client abandons a paged sequence by sending a request with size set to zero and the last cookie returned. The LDAP Abandon operation MAY be used for one request in progress, but this is discouraged as it MAY invalidate the cookie.

If a server cannot resume a paged search, it SHOULD return the appropriate error in searchResultDone, and both sides then treat the result set as closed. A server that limits outstanding paged searches per client MAY return unwillingToPerform for a new one, or age out an older result set, in which case it SHOULD return unwilling to perform if the client tries to resume it.

A client may assume each matching entry is returned once and only once, unless the result set changed since the first request. If it changed, the client may see an entry several times or miss some entries.
sections.plainLanguage: If you say stop, the line ends. If the pile of cards changes while you are being handed pages, you might see a card twice or miss one.

sections.title: X.500 Mapping and Security
sections.content:
For LDAP servers fronting X.500 (93) directories, the control may be mapped onto the X.500 PagedResultsRequest of X.511. The size maps to pageSize and the cookie to queryReference. The sortKeys and reverse fields are excluded.

Server implementors should consider the resources used by paged searches so that misuse does not lock out other legitimate operations. Servers may enforce an overriding size limit to prevent retrieval of large portions of a public directory. Because the size estimate reveals how many entries match a filter, servers that run access control checks on entries may need special processing.
sections.plainLanguage: The server has to make sure one kid asking for page after page does not hog the librarian, and must not reveal secret books just by saying how many there are.
